```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = TRUE,
  fig.dim = c(6, 6),
  dpi = 100,
  out.width = "100%"
)
```

The `data.frame` you provide to the plotting functions must
have a `region` column and a `value` column. The `region`
entries must be INEGI codes for states (e.g., "01", "02") or
municipios (e.g., "01001", "01002"). These codes can be
strings (with or without a leading zero) or numeric. The
package provides the `str_mxstate` and `str_mxmunicipio`
functions to easily format these codes to the INEGI
specification. The package also includes example
`data.frame` objects, such as `df_mxstate_2025` and
`df_mxmunicipio_2025`, which contain demographic variables
from the 2025 Encuesta Intercensal

```{r}
library(mxmaps)
library(htmlTable)

data("df_mxstate_2025")
htmlTable(head(df_mxstate_2025), rnames = FALSE, col.rgroup = c("none", "#F7F7F7"))
data("df_mxmunicipio_2025")
htmlTable(head(df_mxmunicipio_2025), rnames = FALSE, col.rgroup = c("none", "#F7F7F7"))
```

## 2015 Conteo Intercensal

Additional `data.frame` objects are available with data
from other censuses and *conteos intercensales*.

```{r}
data("df_mxstate_2015")
htmlTable(head(df_mxstate_2015), rnames = FALSE, col.rgroup = c("none", "#F7F7F7"))
data("df_mxmunicipio_2015")
htmlTable(head(df_mxmunicipio_2015), rnames = FALSE, col.rgroup = c("none", "#F7F7F7"))
```

The package includes two versions of state names and
abbreviations. This is because common usage often differs
from official names. For example, most people use "Veracruz"
instead of the full official name, "Veracruz de Ignacio de
la Llave." Similarly, the official abbreviation for Chiapas,
"Chis.", can be awkward in some Spanish speaking countries.

## Exporting topojson data

```{r message=FALSE,warning=FALSE}
library("geojsonio")

# Convert the topoJSON to spatial object
data(mxstate.topoJSON)
tmpdir <- tempdir()
# Convert sf to GeoJSON string
geojson_str <- geojsonio::geojson_json(mxstate.topoJSON)
# Convert GeoJSON to TopoJSON
topojson_str <- geojsonio::geo2topo(as.character(geojson_str))
# Write to a file
writeLines(topojson_str, file.path(tmpdir, "state.topojson"))
states <- topojson_read(file.path(tmpdir, "state.topojson"))
```

## String conversion

INEGI municipality identifiers are fixed-width, five-character geographic codes composed of a two-digit state code (Entidad Federativa) followed by a three-digit municipality code (Municipio). The municipality component is zero-padded to a width of three digits, meaning that valid identifiers may contain one or more leading zeros (e.g., 01001, 02003, 09002). Leading zeros are semantically significant and form part of the official identifier; they do not represent insignificant numeric padding. Consequently, INEGI codes should be stored and processed as character strings rather than numeric values. Converting these identifiers to numeric types can strip leading zeros, altering the code and potentially causing referential integrity issues, failed joins, duplicate records, or mismatches

```{r}
str_mxstate(c(32, 5))
str_mxmunicipio(c(32, 5), c(9, 18))
str_mxmunicipio(c(32001, 5009))
```
